text: The assembly will hear an address by Her
Excellency Hilda Heiny, President of the
Republic of the Marshall Islands.
I request protocol to escort her
excellency and invite her to address the
assembly.
Mr. President,
Mr. Mr. Secretary General,
excellencies,
I ask every nation here,
are we still willing to work together?
The principles in the UN charter,
affirmed by each one of us taking our
seat in this hall, are now tested not by
argument, but by neglect or ill
intention.
The credibility and effectiveness of
multilateral institution is imperative
for small nations. It is past time to
better turn the urgency expressed in
polit political declarations and
resolutions into results not repetition.
We speak from our own experience when we
underscore the importance of acting
together.
An institution that takes
decisions collectively must also be
accountable collectively.
Mr. President, the United Nations is
long overdue to reflect and renew the
same spirit with which our Marshal
people first came to the United Nation
by delivering an apology
and acknowledgment of the harm caused by
impacts from the 67 nuclear weapons
tested on our islands during our time as
a UN strategic threat territory between
The sacred trust of the UN trusteeship
to ensure our well-being was jeopardized
by these test and the lack of due
acknowledgement remains a moral failing.
For generations, our families have
testified to displacement,
illness, contamination, and loss. All of
them impacts to our core human rights.
as our survivors would say, and I quote,
"This is a song that has been sung far
too many times." unquote.
It was in the same building that the UN
trusteeship council sat in session and
voted on resolutions
respectively to effectively authorize
further nuclear testing over the demands
of our local leaders and many citizens.
The United Nations ultimately allowed
the testing to continue. But the shock
and tragedy of nuclear exposure in the
Marshall Islands was a profound driver
of the 1963 global ban on atmospheric
testing of nuclear weapons.
We acknowledge the ongoing actions,
dialogues, and complex legacy of the
UN's administering authority, the United
States. But the role of the United
Nations cannot pass without without
comment. For us and for fellow member
states, this apology is an opportunity
to reflect upon the past, to bring
healing and closure to the Marshall
people.
We carry no long no larger agenda other
than to ensure that the United Nations
will do better.
Mr. President, as we face a world in
which scientists tell us overshooting
the 1.5 degree temperature limit that we
agreed in Paris is increasingly likely,
we all need to wake up and act. Our
focus now must be on preventing or
minimizing the overshoot,
shortening the time we spend above 1.5,
and doing everything possible to fight
our way back.
As we gather in Tuvalu, Fiji, and Turkey
for this year's climate, pre-COP, and
COP, our response to the threat of
overshoot must be overwhelming.
A much accelerated transition away from
fossil fuels is the only logical
response.
Continued investment in fossil fuels is
not only immoral but irrational.
Technologies exist which provide secure,
stable, zero emissions energy. We are
employing them in my own country where
in the next 18 months renewable energy
will cut fossil fuel use in our remote
outer islands by 88%.
Giving many access to electricity for
the first time. We must do everything in
our power to accelerate the devel uh
deployment of renewables and to reduce
fossil fuel production and consumption
with equal speed.
This includes shipping shipping where we
have the opportunity at the
International Maritime Organization to
adopt binding regulations that will
place international shipping on a clear
path to net zero by 2050 and generate
the revenue required to ensure a just
and equitable transition.
Mr. President, the denials and delays
that have slowed the transition away
from fossil fuels mean the countries
like mine are already experiencing grave
challenges. We have developed our
national adaptation plan working across
ministries and with our people to
determine how to make a safe future.
Adapting is costly and takes time. Even
as we've seen schools destroyed by
rising seas, saltwater poisoning our
wells, and disease outbreaks linked to
environmental change. This injustice
must be addressed. Our communities
deserve restitution.
The Marshall Islands and vulnerable
people everywhere need sufficient,
timely and accessible finance for
adaptation and loss and damage. Those
who we have profited to the detriment of
the many must pay. We have created
homegrown institutions that are ready
and willing to respond like the Pacific
Resilience Facility, a regionally
managed platform, and the Marshall
Islands Adaptation and Resilient Trust
Fund designed to enable donors to
support our adaptation efforts.
Mr. President, the crisis has the power
to divide us or to prove that we all
remain willing to achieve common goals.
This week, the Marshall Islands convened
the high ambition coalition, a diverse
group of countries committed to a
rigorous response to the climate crisis.
We are united in the view that the best
available science must lead this the
decisions we make. The importance of a
1.5° C temperature limit an urgent
transition away from fossil fuels and
the need for adequate and accessible
climate finance especially for
adaptation and loss and damage.
Mr. President, as a low-lying at all
nation with no higher ground, sea level
rise is an immediate and stark reality.
This week's UN highlevel meeting on sea
level rise has helped achieve new
understanding in international law. It
is the seas that are rising around us
and not our islands which are sinking.
Our boundaries and baselines of today,
the political footprint on the map will
endure in the face of aggressive sea
level rise scenarios.
Our collective stability and security as
Pacific Islands foreign members and as a
UN member state will be now better
addressed.
As an atal nation, our tight cage is
proved enough that far more action is
needed and we are acting. Confronted
with rising seas on our most vulnerable
shorelines, we completed the EBY seaw
wall and foot path last week. 1.8
kilometers of oceanside protection
built with support from the World Bank,
the Green Climate Fund, and our own
resources.
Engineered by rising seas, it now
protects 8,400 people and critical
energy infrastructure.
Reduces annual coastal flooding losses
and anchors resilient future development
on EBY, including schools, housing, and
the proposed new hospital while
providing a safe public space that
strengthens community well-being. It
cost $75 million,
took 70,000 tons of rocks, took more
than a ticket to do, and it is just one
island of over a thousand.
We are taking action, and we urgently
need strengthened partnership to better
protect our islands before sea level
rise overtakes us.
Mr. President, my nation underscores the
importance of the law of the sea as a
key legal pillar of our future. Even
before we were a UN member, we fought
closely both to participate in law UN
law negotiations and to secure these
rights in our constitution.
Pacific Island leadership and that of
all small island developing states has
defined every multi-ateral milestone for
oceans and fisheries and we will
continue to do so. As an ocean people,
the consequences of getting it wrong are
not from distant impacts, but adjacent
to our waters, particularly in the North
Pacific, both within the International
Seabed Authority and unilateral actions.
Collectively, the people and voices of
Micronia must be heard. We are joined by
Guam, Northern Marianas, Federated
States of Micronesia and Palao in
expressing our alarm at seabed mining
actions where the decisions are made
before impacts are well understood and
where adequate safeguard remain
undefined.
The Marshall Islands join 45 nations
seeking a moratorum on seabed mining.
Responsible and science-driven
regulations need to be in place.
Going on guesswork for global oceans is
beyond dangerous. There are no doovers.
The Marshall Islands look forward to the
first conference of parties to the
biodiversity bureau and national
jurisdiction
to work across silos to advance IC's
protection. We urge wide ratification of
the agreement. The Marshall Islands look
forward to supporting its secretariat in
a host nation committed to upholding the
law of the sea as a matter of both
principle and law in words and in
actions.
Mr. President, too often the word
geopolitics is considered to refer only
to the whims of superpowers and not the
reality of our fragile place between
them. As a region of vulnerable island
nations, we read rightly define our own
security priorities and this deeply cut
across every sector, placing a safe
future for our youngest generation
beyond grasp.
As fuel and energy costs are rising
beyond our ability to respond, impacts
from bigger power placed halfway around
the world are amplified tenfold in small
remote economies.
The international community is not
listening closely to small island
developing states and it is not
responding fast enough. Too often the
purported solutions for island nations
don't seem to know the problem.
Mr. President, the Marshall Islands
faces complex challenges in tackling the
SDGs,
but we committed with all of our efforts
to ensure no one is left behind. Our
national planning is now firmly linked
to SDG goals and targets and our actions
proves our commitment. We have developed
direct assistance to vulnerable groups
including mothers and early childhood
development. And we are also reaching
out
to our entire incountry population with
quarterly supplemental income and
improved access to digital finance
tools. Our aspirations must be better
matched by partnership and island scale
investment and policy innovation.
I must underscore the direct need for
data capacity support to measure
progress and effectiveness for small
islands developing states. If we cannot
assist the assess the SDGs, we cannot
correct course. Mr. President, the
Marshall Islands affirms the region
Pacific Islands forum communicate
position regarding West Papua, including
the 2018 invitation by Indonesia
to the UN Human Rights Commissioner.
Further, the Marshall Islands strongly
welcomes recent calls for a ministerial
summit between ASEAN and the Pacific
Islands Forum to take forward our 2020
2023 agreement. Our two regions can
stand united as neighbors and close
friends.
The Marshall Islands affirms it
longstanding support for Japan and its
G4 partners to achieve permanent
membership on the UN Security Council.
Mr. President, the Marshall Islands
expresses its grave concern over
increased efforts to spread spread
dangerous disinformation in these halls.
Taiwan and its 23 million people are an
objective reality and only its
democratically elected government can
represent it. Appropriate ways must be
found for Taiwan's substantive
participation in UN meetings. If the UN
is to be truly inclusive and effective
in years to come, every nation in this
hall may be told that aggression or
coercion upon Taiwan is an internal
matter somehow justified by an ancient
UN seeding chart resolution.
A resolution which doesn't even
reference Taiwan. In years to come, we
may all be told that it's futile for a
small nations to resist a larger one and
that might makes right. Regardless of
the rule book, we all will experience
pressure to accept a false narrative
that UN General Assembly Resolution 2758
somehow serves as a legal pretext under
the UN charter for coercion of or war
impairing freedom of navigation in one
of the world's speciest shipping lanes.
We will be asked politely
and impolitely to turn a blind eye and
look away. It is vital that every nation
here, including our close partners in
our own region, know that know that a
peacemen never satisfies satisfies an
aggressor's wider agenda and one taste
is never enough.
How the UN addresses this very real
security dilemma will be a test of its
strength and relevance.
Excellencies, the Marshall Islands
stands firm in investing ourselves in
this multilateral institution with clear
sight of its frustrations and grave
errors. Two years ago, I concluded my
statement by reciting an old Marshall
proverb.
in Kangal. It describes the coral reef
where different species of fish
congregate to feed and seek shelter.
Today, we are not only being called upon
to revitalize this 81-year-old
institution created from the ashes of
global conflict. But we are being
challenged to address the complexities
of a rapidly changing world. The United
Nations must continue to serve as our
primary wearin kangal to ensure that no
one is left behind.
Thank you.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the president of the republic of
the Marshall Islands.
